subject: radiology
title: Trauma and solid-organ embolisation

steps.tx: Stable trauma bleeding is assessed for embolisation while unstable bleeding goes to theatre. **Arterial phase CT** sorts stable pelvic and solid organ bleeders into embolisation candidates quickly. A **contrast blush** with falling haemoglobin marks active bleeding that is worth coiling. Patients who stabilise and then deteriorate suit a hybrid pathway with surgeons nearby. Blood based **damage control resuscitation** runs alongside mapping and is never delayed until afterwards.
steps.say: Stable trauma bleeding is assessed for embolisation while unstable bleeding goes to theatre. Arterial phase CT sorts stable organ bleeders into suitable candidates quickly. A contrast blush with falling haemoglobin marks bleeding that needs coiling. Blood based resuscitation runs alongside mapping and is never delayed until imaging finishes in emergencies.

steps.tx: The axial contrast CT shows disrupted **splenic parenchyma** with a dark laceration crossing the spleen. A bright round **arterial blush** is circled beside the injury and marks active bleeding inside the spleen. That blush is labelled as the **embolisation target** for urgent catheter treatment. Examiners use this sign to select stable trauma patients for spleen saving embolisation.
steps.say: The axial CT is clear because a splenic laceration disrupts normal parenchyma visibly. A bright arterial blush is circled and marks active bleeding inside. That blush is the target for urgent catheter embolisation treatment. Examiners use this sign to select stable patients for spleen saving embolisation rather than surgery.

vis.alt: Axial contrast CT of upper abdomen showing splenic parenchyma disruption and circled arterial blush.
vis.caption: Axial CT shows splenic injury with arterial blush circled as embolisation target. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: The spleen can survive embolisation because collateral flow keeps it alive. **Proximal splenic coiling** drops perfusion pressure so torn branches clot while the spleen stays viable. A focal pseudoaneurysm with an intact trunk suits **distal superselective coils** instead. Vaccination is needed after splenectomy only, because an embolised spleen keeps immune function. Falling haemoglobin or repeat imaging detects **rebleeding** before collapse develops.
steps.say: The spleen can survive embolisation because collateral flow keeps it alive. Proximal coiling drops pressure so torn branches clot naturally. A focal sac with an intact trunk is suitable for distal coils instead. Vaccination follows removal only because an embolised spleen keeps immune function and protects the patient.

steps.tx: Liver and kidney injuries forgive carefully placed distal embolisation. A **hepatic pseudoaneurysm** is packed while preserving the parent artery where possible. **Renal segmental coils** sacrifice a bleeding pole while sparing the remaining filtering tissue. Unstable pelvic bleeding goes to theatre for packing, while a stable blush goes to radiology for coils. A urine or bile collection that compresses or infects is drained percutaneously for control.
steps.say: Liver and kidney injuries forgive carefully placed distal embolisation. A hepatic sac is packed while the parent artery is preserved. Renal coils sacrifice a bleeding pole and spare filtering tissue deliberately. Unstable pelvic bleeding needs theatre packing, while compressing collections need percutaneous drainage for control and relief.

vis.alt: Diagram showing embolization for hepatic pseudoaneurysms, renal segmental bleeding, and pelvic trauma, with percutaneous drainage of urinoma/biloma.
vis.caption: Liver, kidney, and pelvic trauma embolization strategies

steps.tx: Follow up proves that the organ save has lasted after embolisation. **Repeat CT** before discharge confirms sealed blushes and viable organs in high grade injuries. **Activity restriction** for some weeks protects healing spleens and livers from second rupture. Antibiotics accompany embolisation for open pelvic fractures where contamination is present. Team review audits every embolised case so timing and selection improve for the next patient.
